title: Built-in try for Go error checks

events.summary: A Go team member opens the proposal for a `try` built-in that returns early from the enclosing function when the final error result is non-nil, with error wrapping left to `defer` and library helpers; the text links a design doc, the `tryhard` tool, and later summaries, and notes it was closed.
A maintainer backs the minimal approach but suggests a postfix `?` operator, as Rust adopted, may read better than a built-in function.
A maintainer asks whether named results set before `try` fails are kept, and whether the error result must be named.
A Go team member answers that named results keep their values and the error result only needs a name when a deferred function refers to it.
A maintainer objects to a built-in function altering caller control flow and prefers `?`; the comment was later struck through.
A Go team member points out that `panic` and `recover` are built-ins that already affect control flow.
A user calls the change unnecessary sugar driven by vocal critics and says only error-wrapping helpers are missing.
A user asks what `try` would do with a function returning two errors.
The maintainer withdraws the control-flow objection, regrets responding before the full design doc was out, and says `try` is the least bad option though simplification is not needed.
A contributor doubts error handling needs simplifying, saying it turns vertical complexity into horizontal, but would pick `try` if forced.
A contributor asks for a rewrite tool so people can see how `try` would apply to their own code, ease migration, and examine the effects.
A user worries that a bare `try` call hides the visual cue that control flow may exit and would need IDE highlighting.
A contributor shows that the `defer` wrapping pattern fails with an unnamed local error variable and finds an explicit `if` clearer.
A user likes the idea but argues that a common function exit without a `return` keyword will harm readability, citing a clearly structured CopyFile example.
A user points to an existing AST preprocessor that implemented `try` years earlier.
A user calls it the most Go-like option so far but worries about debugging, since `try` must be unwrapped into `if` blocks to add breakpoints or prints.
A user warns that the `defer` wrapping pattern silently fails without a named result and beginners will trip on it.
A Go team member replies that removing repetitive returns is the point, readers will learn to spot `try`, and people who want explicit returns can skip it.
A contributor worries the design pushes named results and discourages adding context to errors, and suggests a `check` form that takes the error variable instead.
A contributor suggests also allowing `func main() error` to simplify small scripts.
A user argues that the `panic` comparison fails because panics are rare, intuitive and catastrophic, unlike an everyday `try`.
A contributor shares the concerns about named results and lost error context, noting the timing alongside new error-wrapping features.
A user welcomes the fact that `try` rules out try/catch exceptions.
A contributor who now decorates every error says the proposal would force named results and would rarely fit his code.
A user urges the Go team to prioritise generics over error handling, and argues `try` shares the faults of the earlier check/handle draft, preferring assignment-style syntax.
A user suggests using Rust's `?` instead.
A maintainer suggests marking the error result in the signature so the implicit bindings of `try` become visible.
A user argues that since `try` can return it should be a statement-like keyword, not function-call syntax.
A user fears the cost of a subtle, easily missed exit point and says the design makes unwrapped errors the default and wrapping opt-in.
A user worries `try` will become the social default, making richer error paths look improper to linters and reviewers.
A user cites the 'errors are values' principle and argues errors should not be treated like exceptions.
A user opposes the proposal because the boilerplate is not a problem for him and his error handling varies too much for one shortcut.
A user notes `panic` always stands alone on a line, unlike `try`, and would prefer any new flow construct be a leading statement.
A user says nested `try` calls obscure control flow and that libraries adopting it would push his company away from Go 2.
A contributor dislikes the name `try`, prefers `pass`, and finds a hidden return mid-expression hard to review.
A maintainer says it adds a second way to do the same thing and would reduce simplicity.
A user questions saving a few lines and fears hidden handling will encourage lazy, buggy code.
A user whose company adopted the `defer` pattern in anticipation of check/handle says that draft was more complete and its handler scope fit Go better than `defer`.
A contributor calls magic built-ins with inexpressible signatures an escape hatch that avoids real language evolution.
A maintainer disputes that readers will learn to spot `try`, since `return` always starts a line while `try` can nest anywhere.
A user likens `try` to a special-cased macro.
A user replies that `try(` is just as searchable as `return`.
A user clarifies the point was visual scanning, since returns always sit at the start of a line.
A contributor argues `try` merely moves the clutter, the status quo is fine with better tooling, and `if err != nil` reads better.
A contributor objects that `try` nests code inside calls and lets a function exit mid-statement, and votes no.
A user says error handling deserves care and a magic shortcut for bare returns will spread unannotated errors everywhere.
A user replies that people with different per-call handling can simply not use `try`.
A contributor contrasts `try` as an expression usable anywhere with `panic` and `recover`, which effectively act as statements.
A user who reads much Go says `try` will split code style or invite linters, and is only less typing.
A user rejects the 'nobody forces you to use it' answer, since colleagues' code will use it, and says `try` reverses Go's explicitness.
A contributor says `try` makes it easy to cram logic into one line and nested calls are hard to read.
A Go team member notes the many repeated comments and asks people to use emoji reactions instead of restating points.
A maintainer sketches one generic deferred handler helper, possibly made a semi-magic built-in, instead of many wrapping functions.

A Go team member posts a first summary: some welcome the simplification, while the main concerns are that it promotes quick exits over good error handling, hides control flow, and leans on named results and `defer`; he lists suggested alternatives.
A user suggests analysing public Go code to see how many error checks are truly repetitive versus adding context.
A user measures that the targeted boilerplate is about 1.4% of his own code and about 0.5% of the Go repository, questioning the priority.
A user likes `try` on its own line and suggests an optional handler function argument.
A maintainer warns that as an expression `try` invites nested functional-style chains.
A contributor supports the proposal because it avoids the overlap between `handle` and `defer`, and notes it eases adding stack traces and other use cases.
A maintainer notes `check(err)` would read better than `try(err)` and that the definition permits odd forms.
A Go team member says `try` could take an extra handler argument of type `func(error) error` but prefers keeping it simple.
A user writes a long critique, including concern that overloading `defer` for error handling is alarming.
A user suggests a special identifier such as `#` on the left of an assignment to trigger an error return.
A contributor proposes making `try` jump to an `error:` label like `goto`, removing the need for `defer` decoration and giving a visual clue.
A user lists alternative syntaxes for named handlers that check/handle feedback had requested.
A user dislikes punctuation-heavy alternatives that would make Go resemble Perl.
A user prefers handling written after the error and proposes another handler syntax.
A user searches several large codebases for `try` as an identifier and argues a keyword would be acceptable instead of a built-in.
A contributor stresses that `try` mixes a conditional return into an expression, unlike any existing construct.
A user objects with a short 'if it is not broken, do not fix it' code joke.
A user proposes `try` as a keyword restricted to its own line.
A maintainer suggests making `try` a statement rather than an expression to keep exit points visible.
A maintainer reads a few hundred standard-library error returns and reports `try` makes most a bit clearer and under one in ten would nest it in another expression, with examples.
A maintainer says the examples made him take the readability objections seriously and rewrites them with a statement form of `try`, which he finds clearer.
A maintainer thanks the reviewer of real examples and discusses whether `if try` should be legal under the statement idea.
A contributor agrees with another user that each converted example became less clear and more error-prone.
A user agrees the examples hide exit points and rewrites them under a stricter keyword-at-line-start variant for comparison.
A maintainer notes that `defer` handling forces a named error and introduces a new form of nil-check boilerplate, plus deferred and plain versions of helpers.
A contributor commends the standard-library review but concludes the converted snippets are harder to read and easy to misread.
A maintainer explains his `catch` block idea, which names the error locally and so works with plain `fmt.Errorf`.

A Go team member posts a second summary: a built-in is widely felt to be the wrong form and should at least be a keyword or statement, concerns about error context and named results persist, and many alternatives are listed.
A maintainer compares expression and statement `try`-`else` forms with a built-in taking a handler.
A Go team member asks readers to glaze over `try` the way they already skim nil checks, expecting its control flow to become second nature.
A maintainer replies that nil checks still register instantly by shape, and a `try` statement would be easy to skim yet hard to miss.
A maintainer suggests a decoration function after `else` in a statement form, with helper constructors.
A user favours `try` as a statement, which stays explicit and in a fixed position, and calls named-result wrapping a clever hack.
A contributor argues bad nested code should be policed by review and norms rather than distorting the language.
A user suggests a block form of `try` covering several statements for greater boilerplate reduction.
A user posts a loop example handling errors without returning, to contrast with `try`.
A maintainer notes a keyword `try` could count as a terminating statement.
The maintainer concedes that terminating-statement idea is rarely reliable and not worth it.

A Go team member asks to refocus: the thread is about this specific design, not a call for new syntax, and is dominated by a dozen people drafting alternatives; feedback should address the proposal itself.
A Go team member says a design must be judged as a whole rather than by independently rating its aspects.
A Go team lead thanks participants and announces an external page he built to give a navigable view of the thread, updated in batches.
A maintainer asks the design to cover costs and mistakes when switching between error decoration styles and how tooling could help.
A Go team lead says there will be no compiler flags or vet checks to disable a feature: if it is bad enough to disable it will not be added.
A Go team lead says many counter-proposals duplicate the `if` statement, which is already a capable error construct, and the goal is lighter error checks.
A Go team member releases the `tryhard` tool, which finds over 5000 candidate sites in the standard library, and invites people to run it.
A bot links a change applying `tryhard` rewrites to the Go source tree.
A user attributes the criticism to high expectations set by the more comprehensive check/handle draft.
A user argues the change is engineering for its own sake, error handling is not broken, and it trades readability for convenience, possibly to attract enterprise developers.
A Go team lead rejects the idea that some developers are less deserving and disputes the claim about motives.
A Go team member says the proposal never called error handling broken, only verbose, and disputes several of the user's claims.
A Go team lead discusses error context, saying any solution should make adding context more likely and arguing `try` with deferred helpers can do so.
A maintainer says he too sees no problem with current error code and asks how older Go versions would handle code using `try`.
A maintainer explains that the `go` directive in `go.mod` would gate language features by version.
The other maintainer says he does not use modules and cannot follow the explanation.
A maintainer says older toolchains would report an undefined `try` with a note about the required Go version.
A maintainer asks whether a helper package of wrapping functions would accompany handlers if they were added later.
The maintainer says the scenario is hypothetical and hard to assess without modules.
A user objects to being told to move on and argues the proposal solves a non-existent problem at the cost of reliability.
A Go team member repeats that experience with `try` in real code is now worth more than further debate, and asks for experience reports on the feedback wiki.
A user argues the community has spoken: a separate 'leave it alone' issue has far more upvotes than this one, which has more downvotes than upvotes.
A contributor replies that Go is not designed by committee or popularity and the stewards should decide on the data.
A user reports 933 `tryhard` candidates in his company's tools and supports `try` for enforcing a consistent error pattern.
A user calls it a bad idea, citing implicit error variables, ugly `defer` code and a well-known essay on handling errors gracefully.
A contributor reports `tryhard` statistics on his company's code: about 2% fewer lines, with 39% of `if` statements being error checks and 70% of those `try` candidates.
A maintainer illustrates that `try` would let several fallible calls share one `if` condition.
A maintainer doubts a built-in would absorb `fmt`-style formatting and notes a handler argument could cover that need.
A Go team member releases an improved `tryhard` with summary statistics, showing for the Go repository how many functions return errors and how many nil checks are `try` candidates.
A bot links a second change applying `tryhard` to the Go source tree with new options.
A user from a large cloud provider opposes `try` on balance, praising the minimal design but citing Go's readability and simplicity.
A user who reads much unfamiliar code finds `if err != nil` easy to read and says `try` is premature until error wrapping and generics have matured.

A Go team member explains the proposal sits at the feedback stage of the Go 2 process, says only one technical flaw was found and fixed, values data-backed comments over sentiment, and says a few dozen vocal opponents dominate the thread.
A user explains his downvote: he prefers a keyword, would rename it `guard` or `ensure`, and would rather leave `if err != nil` alone.
A maintainer posts `tryhard` statistics for 20 popular packages, with a median of 58% of error checks being candidates.
A user proposes a compact single-line `if err return ...` form instead.
A user insists it should not be a built-in function, comparing it to writing `go` as a function call.
A user replies that a function-call form of `go` would be acceptable.
A maintainer tries `try` on his own code and finds the inlined version harder to read.
A Go team member shows the same code split into two lines with `try`, arguing compressing everything into one expression is a style choice, not inherent to `try`.
A user asks not to add the magic, fearing it will appear everywhere, and prefers explicit handling.
A user summarises the main objections: horizontal complexity, hard-to-read nesting, invisible returns, worse wrapping, a split community and churn between styles.

A Go team member, writing for the Proposal Review Committee, declines the proposal ahead of the planned schedule, citing the overwhelming response, missed issues with debug prints and code coverage, and many people saying the problem was not worth solving; he asks for experience reports on the wiki.
The issue is closed; the API does not record by whom.
A user thanks the Go team for the work and for listening.
A user thanks the Go team member for his patience.
A user suggests locking the thread.
A user thanks the team and community and praises the engagement.
A user posts a pseudo-syntax for attaching conditional returns to a function.
A user says the outcome shows the community is heard and that declined changes are also improvements.
A user suggests a ternary-like conditional return syntax for future discussion.
A Go team member says they need to understand which aspects of error handling are most problematic, that a small verbosity cut may not justify the cost, and that he is unsure a middle ground exists.
A user argues the feedback suffers self-selection bias, since developers bothered by verbose errors avoid Go.
A Go team member thanks everyone, says the team underestimated the reaction, expects error handling work to wait behind generics, and asks for further discussion to move elsewhere.
A user calls the idea an anti-pattern.
A contributor says the issue should be reopened, calling it the most sensible error proposal.
A user says they would expect keyword syntax without parentheses.
A user proposes `try` with an inline handler block.
A user writing in Chinese says Go's error handling is hard to use and shares a try/catch-style helper built on `recover`.
A user posts an image without text, years after closing.
